scripts.opening:opening:
[measured] The Battle of Fort Dearborn.

[short pause] Spring 1812, where the Chicago River meets Lake Michigan. The nearest American post is Fort Wayne, far to the south-east; Detroit, where the general commands, is farther still. [short pause] War with Britain is coming, and every report that reaches the fort makes it feel smaller and farther from help.

[short pause] Seventeen stops follow it in the order it happened, each at its own hour and season.

[short pause] The story begins with the fort, on the afternoon of 6 April 1812.
scripts.stop:the-fort: [measured] 6 April 1812, afternoon, before the fort. [short pause] This story begins here. In the summer of 1803 Captain John Whistler's company marched in from Detroit and built it in logs: barracks round a small parade, 'Two blockhouses' and 'a double row of palisades'. It has stood for nine years. [short pause] Since 1810 it has been commanded by Captain Nathan Heald, with fifty-four regular soldiers. [short pause] Across the river lives John Kinzie, the trader who supplies the garrison, with his family and his clerks; his stepdaughter Margaret is married to the fort's lieutenant, Linai Helm. [short pause] A handful of other families live along the banks: the Ouilmettes, the Burnses, and the hands at Charles Lee's farm. [short pause] The situation is about to ignite, three miles up the river, a little before sunset.
scripts.stop:hardscrabble: [measured] A few hours later. [short pause] 6 April 1812, a little before sunset. Three miles up the river's South Branch is a farm called Lee's Place, later known as Hardscrabble. [short pause] Charles Lee, who 'did not live on the premises, but occupied a house near the fort', owns it; it grows food the garrison buys. [short pause] In the log house are Liberty White, who runs the farm, a discharged soldier, a Canadian hand and Lee's young son. Eleven armed men walk in and sit down. [short pause] Captain Heald wrote ten days later that they were 'supposed to be Winnebagoes'. Sensing trouble, the soldier 'pointed to the cattle which were standing among the haystacks on the opposite bank, and made signs that they must go and fodder them'. [short pause] He and the boy walk down to the canoes and paddle across.
scripts.stop:the-haystacks: [gravely] Ten minutes later. [short pause] 6 April, sunset, across the river from Lee's Place. Out of sight behind the haystacks, the soldier and the boy do not stop to fodder anything: 'they took to the woods' and make for the fort, three miles away. [short pause] Behind them they hear two shots. In the cabin White and the Canadian are killed. [short pause] The two run on downriver in the dusk, and a family with a day-old baby has no idea what is coming.
scripts.stop:burns: [measured] Thirty minutes later. [short pause] 6 April, dusk. Running downriver toward the fort, the two pause opposite this house, where the Burns family live, and shout across to warn them. [short pause] At the fort Ensign George Ronan, 'a young cadet direct from West Point', takes five or six soldiers upriver in a flat-bottomed scow and brings Mrs. Burns out, 'with her infant of scarcely a day old, upon her bed to the boat'. [short pause] A corporal and six men are still upriver fishing, so 'the commanding officer ordered a cannon to be fired'. [short pause] They row home in the dark past the silent farm, find a scalped body by touch, and reach the gate about eleven at night. Heald enrols fifteen townsmen as militia. For four months the settlement waits behind its guns. [short pause] When the blow comes, it comes as a letter.
scripts.stop:the-order: [measured] Four months later. [short pause] 10 August 1812, morning, on the parade. The United States has been at war with Britain since June, and the British have taken Mackinac, the American post up the lake. [short pause] General William Hull, commanding at Detroit, sends a runner, Winnemac, with a written order for Captain Heald: 'It is with regret I order the Evacuation of your Post owing to the want of Provisions'. [short pause] The arms are to be destroyed, and the goods in the government store given away. [short pause] Wau-Bun says the order 'was read next morning upon parade', and that the officers' 'unanimous advice was, to remain where they were, and fortify themselves as strongly as possible.' Heald chooses to obey. [short pause] Outside the pickets, hundreds of people have already heard, and are gathering to see what Heald will promise them.
scripts.stop:council: [measured] Two days later. [short pause] 12 August, afternoon, on this open ground outside the pickets. Heald wrote that the Potawatomi of the country round 'came in from all quarters in order to receive the goods in the factory store'. [short pause] He meets their leaders in council here and promises them the goods. His own officers will not come: 'Captain Heald alone attended on the part of the military.' [short pause] Instead they take the blockhouses that overlook this esplanade, open the port-holes and point the cannon 'so as to command the whole assembly.' It is a council held under the guns. He has promised the goods. [short pause] He has not said what he means to do with the guns and the whiskey.
scripts.stop:factory: [measured] The next day. [short pause] 13 August, early afternoon. This log building is the factory, the government's trading house. Out of it now goes everything on the shelves: 'blankets, broadcloths, calicoes, paints'. [short pause] Heald adds 'a considerable quantity of provisions which we could not take away with us.' Hull's order said the goods could go to those 'desirous of Escorting you on to Fort Wayne'. [short pause] What Heald keeps back, the guns, the powder and the whiskey, is what matters most to everyone watching. [short pause] That night, inside the walls, Heald does something he hopes no one will notice.
scripts.stop:covered-way: [measured] A few hours later. [short pause] 13 August, evening, from above. A covered way runs from the fort's north-east corner down to the river. 'The same evening the ammunition and liquor were carried, part into the sally-port, and thrown into a well'. [short pause] Muskets are broken up and dropped in after them. The rest of the liquor goes 'as secretly as possible through the northern gate, the heads of the barrels knocked in, and the contents poured into the river.' [short pause] Heald feared they 'would make bad use of it'. It is not secret: the knocking carries, and 'the taste of the water the next morning was, as one expressed it, "strong grog."' [short pause] By morning the river tastes of whiskey, and a rider from Fort Wayne is nearly at the gate.
scripts.stop:the-gate: [measured] A day later. [short pause] 14 August, sunset, at the main gate. Captain William Wells rides in from Fort Wayne with a Miami escort, Heald says 'about 30 Miamies'. [short pause] Wells is Rebekah Heald's uncle; he has come to bring her and her husband out, but Wau-Bun says 'all too late': the ammunition is already destroyed. His niece and Heald take him in to Heald's quarters. [short pause] At nine tomorrow the gate will open, and everyone inside will walk out of it.
scripts.stop:the-medal: [solemnly] That evening. [short pause] 14 August, evening, at Heald's quarters on the parade. Black Partridge, 'a Pottawatomie chief from the Illinois River', has come to the fort. [short pause] He 'entered the quarters of the commanding officer' and hands back his peace medal: 'I will not wear a token of peace while I am compelled to act as an enemy.' [short pause] Helm and Griffith both record his warning, and 'Helm alone mentions the surrender of the medal.' It is the plainest warning anyone gives. [short pause] At nine tomorrow the column marches.
scripts.stop:river-mouth: [solemnly] Fourteen hours later. [short pause] 15 August 1812, nine in the morning. 'On the 15th, at 9 o'clock in the morning, we commenced our march', Heald wrote. [short pause] Out of the gate, down to the river's mouth here, and south along the beach: Wells and part of the Miami escort in front, then the fifty-four regulars, the wagons with the women and children, and the twelve townsmen of the militia. [short pause] Wau-Bun says the band played the Dead March, and that Wells 'had blackened his face before leaving the garrison, in token of his impending fate.' The Kinzie family's boat, warned, waits at this river mouth. [short pause] A mile and a half ahead, behind the sand bank, men are waiting.
scripts.stop:the-bank: [gravely] One hour later. [short pause] About ten in the morning, two miles down the beach, with 'the lake on our left, and a high sand bank on our right'. [short pause] 'We had proceeded about a mile and a half,' Heald wrote, 'when it was discovered that the Indians were prepared to attack us from behind the bank.' [short pause] His own journal says 'two miles from the Fort', and the Kinzies later pointed to two cottonwoods here, 'near the place where the attack began'. The soldiers charge up the bank. [short pause] Behind them, at the wagons, Quaife writes, 'a deadlier combat, which we may perhaps think of as a separate battle,' is raging. The militia are 'cut down to a man'. [short pause] Among the dead are 'Cicely, Mrs. Heald's negro serving-woman' and 'her infant son', two of the few people recorded as held in slavery at Chicago. [short pause] Heald has a few dozen men left standing.
scripts.stop:cottonwoods: [gravely] Thirty minutes later. [short pause] About half past ten. Heald gathers his last men on 'a small elevation in the open prarie', out of shot of the bank; the Kinzies remembered that 'the combatants moved south and west over considerable space'. [short pause] A Potawatomi leader called Black Bird comes out, shakes his hand and asks him to surrender, 'promising to spare the lives of all the prisoners.' Heald agrees. [short pause] His count: 'twenty-six regulars and all the militia were killed in the action, with two women and twelve children.' Among them are Ensign Ronan, the young surgeon's mate Isaac Van Voorhis, and Captain Wells. [short pause] Twenty-three years later a boy named Fernando Jones was shown this ground by people 'who were children at the time'. [short pause] The survivors are led back north, and at the Kinzie house the danger is not over.
scripts.stop:kinzie-house: [softly] Eight hours later. [short pause] 15 August, sunset, at the house of John Kinzie, the trader who sold to the garrison. His family is spared and brought home under guard: 'At their own mansion the family of Mr. Kinzie were closely guarded by their Indian friends.' [short pause] Mrs. Heald, badly wounded, is ransomed by Kinzie's clerk for a mule, and Kinzie takes a ball from her arm 'with his penknife.' The gate of the green is open. [short pause] Across the river the fort stands empty; in the morning it will burn.
scripts.stop:the-burning: [measured] The next morning. [short pause] 16 August, the next morning, before the main gate. The garrison marched out of it yesterday and never came back. [short pause] All night the empty fort has been stripped and the plunder shared out: 'shawls, ribbons, and feathers fluttered about in all directions', and one young man struts in 'a muslin gown and the bonnet of one of the ladies'. [short pause] Now the young men come up from the camps with brands from their fires. 'The following morning, the work of plunder being completed, the Indians set fire to the fort.' [short pause] Barracks, blockhouses and the double row of pickets, nine summers of Whistler's squared logs, catch one after another. [short pause] Heald's report gives it one line: 'The next morning, they set fire to the fort and left the place, taking the prisoners with them.' The little brick magazine 'alone defied the fire'. [short pause] Take a brand and put it to the logs yourself.
scripts.stop:war-party: [measured] Thirty minutes later. [short pause] 16 August, morning, back at the Kinzie house, with the fort burning across the river. Black Partridge, Waubansee and Keepotah keep the porch as sentinels. [short pause] Then a party from the Wabash, who have 'blackened their faces', come into the parlor and 'seated themselves upon the floor in silence'. [short pause] Billy Caldwell, the Sauganash, 'entered the parlor with a calm step' and greets them as friends, and, 'thus taken by surprise', they say they came only for 'some white cotton in which to wrap their dead before interring them.' [short pause] A few doors west, a wounded woman is hiding, and men are searching the houses.
scripts.stop:ouilmette: [softly] Thirty minutes later. [short pause] 16 August, morning, while the fort burns. Margaret Helm, Kinzie's stepdaughter and Lieutenant Helm's wife, wounded at the wagons, has been brought here to Ouilmette's house by Black Partridge in 'the ordinary dress of a Frenchwoman of the country'. [short pause] When searchers come, the family 'raised a large feather bed and placed her under the edge of it, upon the bedstead, with her face to the wall', and Mrs. Bisson sits sewing on the front of the bed. [short pause] 'I can but die,' said she; 'let them put an end to my misery at once.' The searchers look round 'and left the house.' [short pause] Quaife doubts the romance, not the rescue.
scripts.ending:burning: [measured] Still 16 August 1812, and the fort you watched them set alight is burning to the ground. [short pause] Heald's report ends the story there: they 'set fire to the fort and left the place, taking the prisoners with them.' Only the brick magazine 'alone defied the fire'. [short pause] On the third day after the battle, the Kinzies were put into a boat for St. Joseph. [short pause] Heald and his wife were taken there too, and the scattered prisoners were held in the villages 'until the following spring, when they were, for the most part, carried to Detroit and ransomed'. [short pause] The army came back in 1816 and built the second Fort Dearborn on the same ground. [short pause] Quaife's warning about Wau-Bun, the family's book that shaped this story for a century: its accounts do Heald 'grave injustice'.
